text:
Game Freak has forgotten what makes Pokemon fun
In a recent interview with Game Informer, composer Junichi Masuda and the director of Pokémon Sun and Moon Shigeru Ohmori were asked if Pokemon will take any inspiration from Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and offer players an open world, freeform experience. The two actually sort of laughed at this question and stated that Pokemon series is more geared towards a storytelling experience rather than games focused on open exploration and discovery.

This made me kinda mad. As a long time fan of the series, the idea that the creators of the series can't see the value in an open world Pokemon experience is incredibly frustrating. It makes it even worse that they think that Pokemon games are fundamentally some kind of rich storytelling experience. When I look back on the history of the series, it makes me think that Game Freak has forgotten what core element holds the series together, and keep players coming back time and time again.

So what makes Pokemon fun?

Is it the story? Doubtful. Even though the latest entry in the series, Sun and Moon, had a more character driven narrative than past games, it's hardly the reason people play Pokemon. It's important to remember that in Red and Blue, the first games in the series, there was almost no story. You just had a rival and an evil corporation that kept getting in your way. Gold and Silver picked up the story a tad, but Ruby and Sapphire were the ones that began tasking players with saving the world from some kind of high concept anomaly (which eventually became a staple in the series). But at its core, Pokemon wasn't founded on its storytelling prowess.

Is it the gameplay then? Closer, but probably not. The series has yet to overall its turn based combat, which is starting to show its age. Pokemon battles are still as tedious as ever, where the player hits a single button, and is rewarded with a 3-5 second attack animation that they've seen hundreds of times before. Although it's undoubtedly a series staple, and can definitely have its fun moments, Pokemon GO has made it clear that it's the concept of Pokemon that gets people excited, not necessarily the turn based combat that the series is known for.

Than what is the core ingredient that makes Pokemon fun? Well I'll just say it, because I can't think of a clever segway: It's the world of Pokemon itself. It's the joy of exploring a whole world of monsters and capturing some of your own. It's traveling a region from coast to coast in the hopes of becoming the best in the land. It's going into dark caves and abandoned buildings and dark forests to discovers legends that you can have for yourself! That’s what gets fans excited when they hear a new game is coming out; the chance to explore a new world filled with new monsters.

And Game Freak thinks Pokemon is about the story? Really? By putting story into the game, you’re effectively breaking immersion by forcing the player to interact with characters and go to new locations regardless of their choice. Red and Blue had no story, and to me, it felt like the most genuine Pokemon experience. That’s because no one was constantly telling you where to go or who to talk to. Now in the new games, you’re set on a certain path with minimal chances for genuine discovery.

I don’t need Pokemon to be exactly like Breath of the Wild, but I at least hope it eventually becomes some type of open world experience. Because my favorite experiences with Pokemon is discovery things all on my own. But now in Sun and Moon, they’ve introduced a mini map with quest markers. And that’s just silly. Because how can you discover anything if you’re not allowed to get lost?

I am sick of loot in games.
So, for the past few weeks, I've been playing through Dishonored 2. It's a great game, and I loved the first, but I often find myself cutting the action and pacing short by insisting on looting/reading every little thing available. Every new building necessitates going through and staring at every desk/table/cabinet and spamming "F" to pick up whatever is found.

Today I booted up Titanfall 2 for the first time, I just got it on sale recently. And holy shit, those three hours just flew by. Nothing to collect (except helmets, but they don't do anything) and the action never stops. It's actually such a blessing.

I felt the same way about Doom 2016. The campaign was great, but the game really shines in Arcade mode, with nothing to loot. Even Bioshock Infinite was kind of a slog to get through with all the loot I needed to pick up. Hell, when I play Dark Souls, I use a checklist just so I don't have to actively search for shit.

Does anyone else feel this way?

text:
I can't stand long animations for picking up items. I've dropped games because of it.
Why do developers feel the need to add tedious, unnecessary animations or wait times to picking up items like plants and rocks? I've dropped Far Cry 3 literally because of this. It's an open world game full of items and crafting materials but you have to hold down the button and wait to pick up the item.

Same for Horizon Zero Dawn. Another open world game full of crafting items but you have to hold down the "pick up" button for 1 or 2 seconds to nab it.

Having a lengthy animation might be great for big, important items like in Ocarina of Time but we're talking about endless trash items all over the world.

And it's not just open world games. I noticed it between Resident Evil 4 and 5. In RE4, you would just pick it up (like money) and there would be an on screen image that you can mash out of. Not ideal but I never felt annoyed by it. Leon never physically grabs the item.

But in Resident Evil 5, there's a dedicated animation. You pick something up and your character physically bends down to grab it or reaches over the counter.

I want devs to stop this. It adds absolutely nothing to the game. These seconds add up especially when there's countless items. If it's to add "realism", I'll remind you this is a video game. This is on par with adding durability to your items (unless your game is about hyper realism). Even medieval combat/weapon YouTubers hate durability.

EDIT

Just remembered about Nier Automata. You have to stop and physically pick up all the chips and items in the world. It's not until 2/3 into the game that you have an item magnet ability. Why didn't they just give us this ability right away?! Item magnetization/vacuuming/auto loot should absolutely be standard in any game where there's endless loot.

text:
Steam Game Festivals are the buffet version of demo discs and should really get more attention.
Demo discs were legendary. My fondest memories of 5th gen are of games I never actually owned and spent tons of time just playing the demos of.

Demos themselves have benefits for the publisher: they generate much more hype/willingness to buy in those who were already interested, they expose new people to the game as with ads, make people who weren't interested more likely to give it a try and perhaps change their mind and they've been used as bonus incentives to buy less popular releases in the past (buy game A for a demo of game B).

Nowadays demos are completely absent when it comes to AAA games and still rare in the indie scene and I've personally completely forgotten all about until I learned about the Steam Game Festival, which is meant to show off new or upcoming indie games, often via demos.

So I've played demos for the first time in over a decade and I have to say - I haven't felt like such an informed customer before. I trie a demo that made me instantly wishlist the game, I tried a demo that was extremely promising and I got to share my thoughts about my concerns with a dev (who gave a response), I tried two that made it clear a game with a clever premise wasn't going to be great, I tried one that looked like someone's first project ever and didn't properly function at all and one that just failed to launch.

If not for the festival, I would only ever hear about one of those games at best and I'd be very hesitant to buy into it. Having a chance to communicate with developers is great too and I feel like because this is a limited time event, they're more likely to dedicate time to keep up with the incoming feedback during this period at least.

My biggest issue with this whole thing is that while a lot of games in the festival have demos, many do not and it's not immediately clear which are which without entering their respective store pages. To me demos are the most important part of the Steam Game Festival and I think it would be reasonable to either make the event either exclusive to games that have those, make separate sections for those who do and do not or introduce some sort of store-wide icon that shows that a game has a demo available without entering its store page.

I have high hopes for the Steam Game Festival. Just like Xbox Games Pass, it has a real chance of introducing people to new stuff and get out of their comfort zone without having to risk a bad purchase. Having demos get more widely spread would be an amazing thing considering how many games release broken nowadays, too.

text:
Assassin's Creed Odyssey is really great, until it suddenly isn't.
I'm sure there have been many posts like this but I feel like putting my 2 cents out there.

I got ACO for free with a video card. Having not played an AC game since Brotherhood, I was pretty excited to see how far the series had come.

It started out pretty cool. Tutorial Island did a great job of introducing game mechanics one at a time. Combat, conversations, exploration, caves, enemy outposts, side quests. Unfortunately your first few interactions with these systems are the best parts.

I believe Ubisoft showed their entire hand a little too early. From the moment you pick up the first batch of quests on the mainland, you already know that this game is rinse and repeat.

Dialogue is boiled down to "good response", "bad response", and "more info". Every single quest is either gather or kill something. Dialogue for side quests is irredeemably repetitive ("So you need me to kill them?" followed by "Your man is dead.")

The environment is gorgeous and the climbing is fun, but there is next to no landscape variety aside from a couple small islands.

The loot system is so saturated with pointless gear that sorting/selling/dismantling your inventory feels like a huge chore. I don't want to spent 15 minutes in my inventory every time I go to town. I will admit that I enjoyed collecting set pieces and playing around with those passive bonuses, but I ended up alternating between 2 sets for the entire game.

Enemy outposts are literally copy and pasted half the time. And once your clear one, it's magically full of the same enemies next time you ride by. The mercenaries system was intriguing at first. It felt very dynamic and I liked the obvious inspiration from the Shadow Of Mordor/War's Nemesis system. However I quickly became disillusioned once I realized that enemy mercenaries literally just sprint across the map towards you then start walking and slowly searching once they get within a certain range of you.

Naval combat was incredible the first 5 or 6 times but again becomes more of a chore once the novelty fades.

And finally the main story I just couldn't stay engaged with. I tried catching up on the total mess of a story behind the AC series but holy fuck what is going on in that writers room. The overarching story is an irrelevant clusterfuck and the main story is nothing special whatsoever. It's a doomsday cult and your sibling is the big bad.

My enjoyment of this game peaked about 15 hours in and then steadily declined. I admit I still got about 60 hours of decent gameplay but at some point I just dropped it completely out of pure boredom. I didn't even finish the game.

Almost every system in this game is wonderful until you become too familiar with it. Wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle, yadda yadda. Does Valhalla fall victim to the same modern tropes?

When i see terrible AI in modern games i'm always bitterly reminded of one particular game that not only did AI well, but in my opinion still hasn't been beaten when it comes to enemy AI: The original F.E.A.R
The enemy AI in this game is absolutely fantastic. Like it's downright absurd how well the AI on the enemy soldiers (called Replicants) are able to use the environment to their advantage as well as able to communicate between each other and are able to determine your position very well. Much of their brilliance can actually be attributed also to the enviromental design itself since from interviews of the developers it was told that the AI was designed around the office style enviroments which allowed the creators to mask how good the AI actually is. And it worked brilliantly. On the harder difficulties it actually feels like you're fighting real players. No two gunfights will ever be the same, no matter how much you replay the game. Sometimes they'll stick to cover, sometimes they'll just bull rush you. Sometimes they'll chuck grenades to force you out of cover. Sometimes they might blindly fire towards you so you get pined down while another flanks you etc. Any FPS or horror fan owes it to themselves to play F.E.A.R 1. It's a masterpiece not only in just the AI, but the excellent gunplay as well. And whilst i said all this i want you to keep one thing in mind. F.E.A.R 1 came out in 2005

text:
I think RPGs would benefit from scaling down their main story
The thought hit me while playing Hades - it's not even part of a genre that's supposed to care about its story, and yet I enjoyed that game's story more than almost every RPG I've played. There are many reasons for it - the writing is clearly better than what we're used to seeing for instance - but I think one key aspect is that despite being about literal Gods and Goddesses, the story feels very close to us and is definitely driven by the characters themselves. Because it's a smaller scale story about a more "real" story, it also gives room to its characters to grow - including the villains, which is much harder to do when said villains' goal is to literally enslave or kill everyone.

For instance I was checking out Baldur's Gate 3's description on Steam and the first sentence mentions the lure of absolute power. So I can already imagine a story similar to DOS2 with some world-threatening power that you have to beat at the end. I'm not saying the story will be bad necessarily (I don't intend to play until the final release in any case) but it's so tiring to basically always see the same damn thing, just reskinned and sometimes a bit more or less grimdark, but always with the same tone and themes. For similar reasons, I'm one of the (few, I think) people who prefered The Witcher 2's story over the third one - because it was much more "grounded" as you mostly fought for yourself and Temeria/the Northern Kingdom, not the entire damn world. And your ennemies were so much more interesting than the angsty Space Elves that the Wild Hunt ended up being. The best story in that game was the Bloody Baron's arc for me, and that part was definitely a lot more relatable than the end.

I get it, most RPGs are set in a classic Heroic Fantasy universe and it's supposed to be an epic story. But I honestly think that it's perfectly possible to create a story that feels epic and satisfies the player's power fantasy without having to be about a world-spanning threat.

Thougths?

Are We Ruining Games by Playing Too Efficiently?
I’ve noticed a weird trend in modern gaming: we’re obsessed with "optimal" playstyles, min-maxing, and efficiency. But does this actually make games less fun?

Take open-world RPGs, for example. Instead of naturally exploring the world, many of us pull up guides and follow the fastest XP farm, best weapon routes, or meta builds. Instead of role-playing, we treat every choice as a math problem. The same happens in multiplayer—if you’re not using the top-tier loadout, you’re at a disadvantage.

I get it, winning and optimizing feels good. But at what cost? Are we speedrunning the experience instead of actually enjoying it? Would gaming be more fun if we all just played worse on purpose?

Is this just how gaming has evolved, or are we killing our own enjoyment?

text:
Valve seriously need to start putting a foot down on indie shovelware/horrendous greenlight and early access games.
So, Goat Simulator - fun game. Not my personal cup of tea, but it has some pretty hilarious moments. It was pretty creative, and did something a bit different. It was very tongue-in-cheek towards the massive simulator game market which has seen a surge in international popularity in recent times, thanks to the Greenlight marketplace.

Now, don't get me wrong - I don't think Goat Simulator is actually a "joke game". It's a funny game, and it's far from AAA Quality; but I wouldn't call it a joke. Actual development time did go into it, and the devs are continuing to work on expanding its feature set, ala the Goat Simulator Online/MMO expansion.

However, in the rise of Goat Simulator, arrived with it the true "joke games"; and like all jokes, they get outrageously tiring when repeated non-stop for what seems like an infinitely expanding amount of time.

Currently, we've got a metric tonne of titles all living off the "x Simulator" joke, which are mostly Unity3D scenes pointed at a couple of prefabs; but by far, the worst I've seen so far is Grass Simulator, retailing at a cozy €9.99. There are currently 134 reviews (mostly negative) - the most unfortunate sign of that being that we can assume at least 134 copies of the game have sold (netting just over €1300); for a prefab scene that would have taken around 1-2 hours to build, at most.

The problem here is that we're currently in an avalanche of joke games, simply due to the fact that people will actually buy them - and for someone struggling with cash who possesses the Unity3D engine, why not dump an hour or two of your time into setting up a quick scene with a few prefabs, throw it on greenlight, and get your rent paid up for the next month? The end result is what Steam is now becoming; a marketplace edging ever closer to Google Play levels of spamware.

And here's the problem - it's us. The gaming community are voting these titles in, while talented developers and their titles need to sit out in obscurity due to the power of the popular vote. Steam used to be a platform that did the filtering for us; when it came to indie games, there was a vetting process that eliminated the horrorware that is "Grass Simulator" and its counterparts. The days of popular indie gaming being associated with masterpieces such as Super Meatboy, Braid, Bastion and the likes is rapidly leaving our shores; and the bar is being set at horrifically low levels for getting your product sold on the Steam Marketplace.

Unfortunately, it's unlikely that Valve would backtrack on their greenlight decision; as a gaming studio whose profits now seem to solely come from publishing, it would be financially a bad decision for them to go back towards a quality-over-quantity approach to gaming.

So, let's discuss - do you think anything can realistically be done to stop the Steam Marketplace from becoming the equivalent of Google Play for PC Gamers? Or are we as gamers, even in a position where we can demand such changes be made to suit our own preferences, or our personal standards in cases such as these?
label: analysis

text:
Are a lot of indie games just glorified online flash games?
I understand that indie doesn't refer to a type of game, but typically indie games have lower production values. Much, much lower production values, to the point where just about every 2D game can easily be identified as indie. Now that doesn't mean they're necessarily worse, but a lot of times you see hype for indie games equivalent to AAA titles. I went on GameSpot and saw an announcement about an indie game coming to XBLA, as if it were any other game being released by a major publisher. A couple days ago there was an AMA from the dev for Gunpoint, and people were raving about how it was such a great game and they'd be sure to buy a copy to support him.

After watching the gameplay, I can honestly say it seems no different from a flash game from the good ol' golden age of flash games about 10 years ago, when Shockwave was huge, and school kids would go to computer labs to get onto addictinggames. The difference is, one costs typically $10-$20 per copy, and the other was free (for the player). One is reviewed in gaming magazines and websites and the other gets a 1-5 star rating from users. One is constantly hailed on reddit and by gaming communities while the other is thrown aside as being casual.

Look at a game like Limbo. The graphics can be recreated in flash. The length is the same as a lot of flash games (2-3 hours for the memorable ones). It's not a particularly super innovative concept. Sure the art style is nice, but style is independent of budget. And yet Limbo sold millions and was highly praised as being super artistic and worth ever dime. So what is it that makes indie games seem like the new direction of video games, while flash games have been tossed aside as cheap casual entertainment to pass the time here and there and never taken seriously?

EDIT: For the record, I own several indie games including Bastion, Meat Boy, Machinarium etc. Please keep the discussion focused on indie vs flash games, not on trying to convince me that indie games are good
label: hot_take

As games get better looking, "invisible walls" are becoming harder to ignore
This is something that has really stood out to me while playing God of War Ragnarok, and in quite a few other games in recent years.

As visuals become more impressive and realistic-looking, it's becoming more difficult for me to suspend my disbelief. Since I'm playing Ragnarok at the moment, I'll mainly focus on it for this topic.

There are so many puzzles I have come across where Kratos could simply step over to the side or climb up a small rock and the "puzzle" would become completely trivial. I find myself thinking constantly, why can't I just climb this gentle slope to get the treasure chest?

I'm also reminded of a puzzle in Darksiders I or II where a gate is blocking your path, but the bars are spaced so far apart, that your character could literally just walk through the gaps if they wanted to.

Anyways, I can't say that this bothers me, but it's something that I've been noticing more and more. Anyone else kind of amused by this "problem" ?

text:
Playing through Cyberpunk 2077 again mad me realize how having different biomes in an Open World game can make the player's experience so much less tedious and boring
Now granted, Cyberpunk isn't the only open world game that does this well, it's just a more recent example, there are a few others that i will mention as well. Cyberpunk has it's issues (most of them fixed by now) but one of the things i absolutely adored about it when it came out, and still do, is the enviroment, or, more precisely how diverse it is.

From the slums in Watson, the giant skyscrappers and corporate shindigs of Corpo Plaza and the city center, the peaceful greenery of North Oak, the abandoned markets of Pacifica, the dystopian Industrial Zone in the south, the homely suburbs of Santo Domingo and the absolute beautiful emptiness of the Badlands. The environmental variety makes going for a drive in this game feel like a cruise instead of something you just have to do to get from point A to B. Entering the Badlands for the first time is easily one of my favorite gaming moment, up there with stepping out of Vault 101 into the Capital Wasteland. The utter instant change of scenery from the busy city streets to just this vast desert open plain caught me so off guard, pleasantly of course and it's proof how much environmental variety adds to an open world. Same thing with games like Fallout 4 and Skyrim as well

text:
Ghost of Tsushima's walking mechanism with companions is what other games should aspire to have.
I'm not really sure if that's the right term "walking mechanism", but whatever...

So I just finished Ghost of Tsushima, and the game is amazing and all that, but what really amazed me the most was the way the characters moved. And by that, I mean the most simplest thing is moving with companions.

Games always seem to have this trouble of properly walking with companions.

I'm sure all of you have encountered this scenario.

It's after a scene, and your companion either asks you to follow, or let you lead the way. Then you both walk. But you want to run. So you do.

But as soon as you start running, you'll noticed that your companion is still just.... walking.... slowly....

So you stop to wait for them to catch up. Then you wisened up and think 'I should just walk as well'. So you do...

BUT your walking speed is COMPLETELY different from your companions. It's always either faster or slower, never the correct pace. You either outpace them, or they outpace you.

It's a mechanism that has always made me go nuts.

And the cherry on top is this is mostly accompanied with dialogue from the characters. And even though you're moving behind/ahead, they're still both talking to each other like they're completely side by side.

Ghost of Tsushima, on the other hand, has fixed this. Both the characters are always correctly paced. If you run, then they run. If you walk, then you walk. If you stop, then they, too, stop. If you mount a horse and then walk or run, they would do the same.

IT WAS GREAT.

I ALMOST NUTTED MYSELF WHEN I SAW THIS.

Because of this, the way they talk is never unnatural. They're literally talking side by side! The dialogue is never awkward to listen to.

Also, one of the best things that I saw is that if the scene demands it, it forcefully makes the characters walk to make sure the dialogue finishes before the next dialogue begins so you don't miss anything at all.

Like, what the heck, why wasn't this thought of before?!

Ghost of Tsushima completely spoiled me in regards to this mechanic, and unless future games do this as well, I think I'll forever hold Ghost of Tsushima in the highest regard concerning this mechanic.

text:
Bethesda needs a REAL competitor in their genre.
To be honest, I generally love Bethesda games. They are just so damn unique, and I really enjoy exploring the worlds they create.

But I've noticed how their games have changed over the years, and I'm...concerned. Especially after Fallout 4. Even after Skyrim and Oblivion I was, but I wasn't too worried because despite the changes, they were still phenomenal games.

I don't know, though. Like I said, I'm not the biggest fan of all the "streamlining". Some of it's okay, and some of it is just pure dumbing down, plain and simple, and the stuff that I think could be cool is overly simplified and implemented poorly, like the perk system.

Bethesda needs a competitor to seek out and actually listen to its more niche players. But it doesn't really have one for it's genre: open world fantasy RPGs based on exploration. Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning? No interest. Studio shut down. Dark Souls isn't exploration based, more on combat. The Witcher series, even the third installment, is focused on the story and not exploration. Fallout series is own by Bethesda. Dragon Age series, similar to the Witcher series, is story based; even Inquisition. Mass Effect, story.

Game series like the Elder Scrolls, the real meat of it that people love, don't exist. The first person aspect, the customization, the soundtrack, the open world, and the ability to explore and do whatever you want, all in a fantasy setting with tons of quests- does this exist anywhere else today? It doesn't seem to.

There are a couple of popular mods called Nehrim and Enderal to Oblivion and Skyrim respectively. These are basically their own complete RPGs, and the closest things to the Elder Scrolls that are made by a different developer and are completely unrelated to the Elder Scrolls world and license.

If Bethesda had a competitor, maybe it would drive them to reach back to their core niche, RPG audience that played Arena, Daggerfall, and Morrowind back in the day.
label: analysis

text:
Why is Elden Ring so successful? Because it makes a hard games *rewarding* instead of *punishing*.
Elden Ring is succesfull beyond belief, cause it has brought the soulsborne formula to a larger audience. However, there is a paradox in there: core to the soulsborne games is that they are hard and core to western game design is that hard games aren't accessible - they aren't what most people want.

So what happened?

Normally hard games are punishing - you die, you try again. If you aren't good enough, you are stuck. Maybe you can grind to become overpowered or maybe you just have to improve your skills or copy a strategy guide. Either way, you can't naturally progress within your playstyle - you can't do the next thing you are interested in cause you have hit a wall.

Now other soulsborne games might have multiple paths through the world but all of them are hard and there arent many. The above still applies.

In comes Elden Ring. Instead of being punishingly hard, it's rewardingly hard. But what is rewardingly hard?

It's when things remain hard without stopping you in your tracks or forcing you down paths you don't want to go. You get the satisfaction of beating challenges while playing the way you want:

Stuck on a boss? Go explore and come back with more levels and gear. Or even forget about him all together.

Disillusioned with your melee build, there are ranged weapons and even incantations that scale off strength.

Not the best fighter? Why not backstab half the castle. Stealth actually matters for once. And failing that, you can play half the game in road rage mode and run out mobs without laying a finger on them, just grabbing their gear and gold runes.

Elden Ring had amazing art, amazing design, amazing game play. But that's not unique. What is unique is that Elden Ring makes a hard game accessible and fun for everyone, no matter your playstyle or skill level. And that's a truly precious item.

text:
Just because you enjoy a game doesn’t mean you shouldn’t criticize it
I’m sure this will stir up some passionate people, and that’s great! We want to generate good discussions. But this is something I’ve seen with many past games, and I’ve already started seeing with Anthem so I wanted to start a discussion about it. Since that’s what’s spawned this post, I’ll be using it as an example but this applies to pretty much all games.

The reviews have started to drop for Anthem, and they seem to be sitting right in the 6-7/10 area. As expected, there are extremes on both sides of the fence with loving and hating the game, but I’ve also seen quite a few “well I’m enjoying it” and it’s these people who I’m mainly focused on. If you enjoy a game, that’s great. You shouldn’t let someone else tell you if you can or can’t enjoy a game, and being able to find joy where others can’t is a great outlook to have. But that being said, “well I’m having fun” is not a valid excuse for bad game design or flawed gameplay systems.

I personally have no interest in Anthem. I played the beta and won’t be buying it, but it’s one of those games where the reception of the game is almost more fascinating than the game itself. And when people love a game, they take that love as doctrine and seem to think that they can’t admit anything is wrong with the game at all, which is just silly. If anything, you should be more critical if you love a game because you know what would make it better and you can see what it could be. The game isn’t even officially released yet, but I’ve seen too many people brush off valid criticism because “well I’m enjoying it”, and I assume they don’t want to look like a “hater”.

Another example is the Witcher 3, which is my favorite game. I know, I know, that’s a real unique take for a favorite game, but it is. But I also have a list a mile long of changes and improvements that I’d make if I could, because nothing is perfect. It has plenty of frustrating design decisions and aspects that make you go “wait, why in the world did they do it that way?”. And for a while I was part of the Witcher subreddit and absolutely loved being among fellow fans, but after the game blew up I eventually had to unsubscribe. “Praise Geraldo” is definitely a bit of a meme, but that was basically gospel on that subreddit. You couldn’t mention anything even remotely wrong with the game without being downvoted to hell and being met with “it’s not that big of a deal”.

I got a bit distracted, but in the end that’s kind of the point I want to make - when you enjoy a game, it’s okay to mention flaws and criticisms. That’s how games improve and get better. Not only will developers not know what to fix if we don’t say anything, but brushing valid criticism under the rug only shows publishers how much they can get away with. The more we allow broken releases and buggy launches, the more they’ll push the envelope. So if you really do love a game that not many others do, thumbs up to you. But don’t write off valid criticism because of some need to defend the game. Amplify the criticism so that you can not only get the issues with your game fixed, but so that we can (hopefully) make game launches better and not let them get worse.

text:
Is the "investigate area + follow the footprints" gameplay trope overdone? What are some alternatives?
I'm about 10 hours into Ghost of Tsushima, and most of it is excellent. The gorgeous world. The fluid combat. The "guiding wind" as a natural replacement for mini-maps and waypoints. But for me, precisely one thing has ground the game to a halt, interrupting the great stuff with a trope that feels years out of date:

"Find clues + follow the footprints!"

It's the classic sidequest formula. Lead player to Point A. Sidequest begins. Look around for clues (usually, a bit of blood, a broken window, a stray arrow, some trampled grass, etc.). Notice footprints. Press action button every 50 feet or so to (yet again) "observe" how the footprints continue along. Eventually come to Point B. Engage in combat. Return to Point A. Collect reward.

Open world games have been doing this for years. The Witcher 3 is among the most well-known examples. You'd use your Witcher senses to see the glowing footprints to nudge you along to the next point of interest. Horizon Zero Dawn had several sidequests exactly like this. Red Dead 2 did this, although to be fair, it was a bit more subtle in that title.

And now Ghost of Tsushima. Look: I get why open world games do this. It's a tried and true way to get your main character to narrate plot points ("There was a struggle! The blood is fresh!"), and it gives the devs an excuse to move players to the next spot. But to me, it was never all that interesting, and now, it's painfully tedious. In my mind, it also wastes the potential of these otherwise innovative worlds.

What could open world games do instead, now that they've beaten the "footpints" gimmick deep into the ground? One example can be found in the same game I'm critiquing: Ghost of Tsushima. For a handful of "Mythic Tales," the game gives you a hand-drawn map with physical landmarks to look out for. You then explore the world yourself, getting to know the topography, staying on alert for the key structures/mountain/rivers, and eventually, you triangulate the location.

This is excellent! It allows the player to continue to form a relationship with the world, rather than mindlessly following footprints. There's no need to click your mouse or hit R2 every 50 feet to reassure the game that yes, you're still following the same very obvious line. It hands the agency back to the player. (RDR2 also does this with some of the treasure hunting, which I thought was also well designed.)

Are you also tired of the footprint gimmick? How do you think games—especially open world games—could do sidequests like this better?

text:
The monetization trend where singleplayer games cripple the player's progress to squeeze out money, like some kind of mobile game
I think this phenomenon started back with Shadow of War. At least that's the earliest example I could remember. You had the end of the story, and then you had the Shadow Wars which had an atrocious difficulty spike that was meant to make you purchase lootboxes to progress further. This system was almost like some kind of mobile game in that the game just scales too fast and doesn't give you the tools to keep up without paying money.

The second time I've seen this happen was less so in AC: Origins and moreso in AC: Odyssey. AC: Odyssey had levels and levelled enemies, and the game intentionally crippled your experience so that you would buy "boosters". The game was intentionally crippled and stripped off a regular progression like any other RPG would give you to make the grind twice as long if you're not willing to pay 10 bucks. Now AC: Valhalla has come out and it's clear Ubisoft is not planning on letting up on this trend if you look at the reviews and people's experiences.

In general the trend seems to be that they offer the player something akin to cheat codes to progress faster. However, this is only what it seems like. In reality, the game's progression is intentionally crippled to the point where it's not as fun to play or grindy like it should only be if it was free or multiplayer. Then you pay money to bring the progression back to what it would be in any normal $60 game.

Imagine if Skyrim halved your skill gains unless you paid 10 bucks. That's what they are doing. They aren't making anything faster for you, they cripple the progression to make it grindy and then you pay to make it normal again.

I find it a very despicable practice, moreso than selling skins or selling microtransactions that are just cheat codes. Because there is a difference between these being optional and yet tempting to a lot of people, and designers purposefully crippling the player's progress so that the game is either a huge timewaster, or just a normal game like it would be without the calculated crippling of progression.

It reminds me of mobile games where your progression gets insanely slow at some point, that then make you buy lootboxes and "optional" purchases to make it faster. It feels like a downwards spiral towards $60 AAA games having mechanics of free games with terrible monetization schemes, like AFK Arena, F:GO and Genshin Impact.

What do you think of this trend? Have you seen it happen in more AAA games lately than the ones I've mentioned? Do you think this trend will continue?

As a new player, World of Warcraft is a really wierd experience.
After the most recent expansion I decided to give WoW a try, I played MMORPGs a long time ago - Everquest, Guild Wars, so I was looking forward to finally experiencing the most successful MMORPG ever.

But right from the start.. it was wierd. The main issue was that the world was empty, dead, in 2 months of play I never really interacted with anyone. Beginner areas, expansion areas (Panda island, Lich Kingn island), and even the capital cities other than people AFK outside auction houses. I stopped playing because I realised it was basically a single player game with old fashioned combat.

Progression also seemed broken - everything was very easy to kill and you really needed to be brain damaged to die. Yet at the same time there was no sense of getting stronger because enemies seemed to scale with me, so even after +20 levels the combat was similar. In fact levels seemed pointless in general - at the start I gained new spells and skills, but then each level became meaningless - nothing gained, nothing changed. The most extreme example of broken scaling were some of the raids - I couldn't find any groups so I tried solo entering raids - where I could aggro hundreds of mobs and slay them all in one AOE hit.

Other social aspects seemed dead - joined two guilds where nobody talked, and chat channels were silent. I like MMORPGs so I'm surprised that it was so antisocial, its not what I expected at all.

I guess the game is entirely designed around existing players, but in that case what is the point of all these empty areas? Or old raids where you can 1 shot entire armies? Why not just remove them? There was an option to start at max level, but that doesnt negate how pointless 90% of the world was. The best way I can describe WoW is it felt like visiting an empty virtual museum.

text:
Temporary events don't excite me or encourage me to log into a game; they make me anxious.
No Mans Sky Expeditions, temporary season passes with rewards, special mounts that drop from bosses, and transient content of that nature do not motivate me to revisit a game; they stress me out because it forces me to schedule time to play a game instead of revisit them on my own terms when I am able.

They recently added the Normandy to NMS as a reward for completing the latest Expedition. This is great if you actively play NMS, at least have it installed, or are otherwise flexible enough to make time for it in the limited (10 day) window.

But I won't even say it's the limited window that's the issue. Rather, it's the transient nature of the content that makes me think "why bother?" The content exists and it doesn't actually need to be removed once implemented. That content will perpetually exist in the code base and so the impetus is purely artificial and comes off as kind of a scam: You paid for the game and updates but are artificially held hostage by this design.

So, no, while I would love the Normandy in my fleet the stress that this and likely future content is limited does not make me want to play your game. It's cool, but it's not fun. I play games to relax not to get stressed out by deadlines; I get enough of that at work.

I think I may have actually reinstalled NMS and I may try to play but clicking launch now bears a burden that didn't exist a decade ago. Games aren't meant to induce stress for avoidable reasons.

There is a crowd out there that will advocate that this makes the content more special to them because it is limited and future players will not have access to it. However, this train of thought is a bit anti-social:

I think all players should be able to enjoy and access content on their own terms. It may actually be an accessibility issue. I am sure I am not the only one that gets a little triggered by this whether they realize it or not.

I just wish this trend would die. Urgency is one of the oldest sales tactics in the book and it is cousins with loot boxes and gacha mechanics. It has no place in games because it grooms users to make time for a product they already own and should have full agency over.

text:
Dear Players: Please be mindful of how you request features
Hello! I'm a solo game developer. My particular project is very community focused, and I've always encouraged player collaboration and fostered an inclusive community. I love my players, they're the reason I'm able to do this, and the reason anyone knows about my game. For the most part, I couldn't ask for a better community. But today I am here to vent.

To begin, here is a list of the ways in which feature requests or game questions reach me:

My work email

My game's subreddit

The comments on the subreddit

My Reddit PMs

My Discord PMs

Pings on Discord (constantly)

My Twitter PMs

My Facebook PMs

My Twitch PMs

The Steam forums

Comments in YT threads that I participate in

Forwarded to me from my Community Manager who receives PMs

Forwarded to me from my Publisher who receives PMs

In person at events

In bug reports ( ?! )

Sometimes, my actual feature request website (yay!)

I will point out that these often reach me whether or not I am working. I'll see them trying to just browse Reddit or use Discord for fun. If you're a small game company, your social media thread is awash with your own game by necessity. It's all you can do to take a moment to to think of anything other than the massive, insurmountable seeming project that already dominates your life.

I am one person. I have 100,000 players. I love you, but I can't make time for all of you.

So, dear players, my request: Most developers probably have a proper channel or format for submitting player feedback. Please, please be mindful in the manner of which you give feedback and requests, especially to small developers. It will do wonders for their sanity. And thanks for listening.

EDIT: Thanks for all of the advice I am taking it to heart. I think the best answer to avoid this in the first place is for the game to have an integrated way to submit feedback. Then, everything points there.

That said, I think I haven't been clear; My intention was not to solve my problem by complaining, or to change the behavior of players for my sake. It was meant to be more of a PSA (plus vent). If players submit feedback through appropriate channels, they're more likely to be heard, too.

But yeah, at the end of the day, the onus to prevent this reality is on me. Hopefully other start ups can learn from my mistakes!
label: hot_take

Does anyone else here get sort of 'waves' of disinterest with a game they are playing? Like they hit a new level and suddenly all interest for the game just disappears and you want to end it? Keep going, it will pass.
Honestly, this has really changed my perspective quite a lot in terms of gaming and made my experience a lot better. For a lot of people, we 'quit' the moment we get even slightly bored with a game, so we only get a few hours in before quitting. This leaves us with countless games that we have only gotten maybe 15% in in terms of progress, never to be finished.

For me at least, and I am sure many others, there is a certain moment where I will just get a wave of disinterest and boredom with whatever I am doing. Usually it happens when I hit a new level. Everything in your body is telling you to alt-f4 out of there and do something else.

Don't fall for it. The wave passes. Even if its difficult to continue for a few minutes, its best to just force yourself through it. I know that it sounds stupid, you're supposed to be enjoying the game so why would you force yourself to do it if you don't want to? But its more that it gives you more satisfaction in the long run.

This has honestly made it so that my interest and dedication to games is way, way better. It also just makes games more enjoyable overall, it really was disheartening before how quickly I would give up games.

text:
Is there a specific name for 'static' game design set ups?
I was thinking about how a lot of games, particularly ones that come form the 2000-2010's era of gaming, have become lite-RPG-ized in their design. What I mean by this is like in the most recent example of Gears of War Eday.

In the classic Gears games, you basically had a set amount of abilities, and your character didn't really improve those abilities. Which is to say, you start out with a lancer, a gnasher, a snub, and the typical assortment of character abilities (melee, roady run, evade roll, etc). There were no levels, mods, or extra abilities you got intrinsically, the most you got to expand your combat abilities is whatever a level offered, like new guns or a turret section, etc.

In Gears Eday, you have mods that you unlock as you go through the game. You got passive armor mods, you got an ultimate ability, and you got 3 mods slots for all your weapons. This is to say, in classic Gears, your lancer was as powerful at the end of the game as it was at the starat of the game, but in Eday, you could give it a different set of abilities by the end.

This is a trend I've noticed with a number of genres though. Classic Halo also had a static set of abilities, but Halo Infinite has you picking various abilities and stat enhancements. Classic God of War games had levels to their weapons/magic, but the new GoW games are straight up lite-action RPG's. Uncharted is a less conventional example, but even there, you get a pike that helps you climb things about halfway through the game, where classic Uncharteds you had the same static climbing abilties the whole game.

So, is there a specific term for this old school type of game design that seems like devs have abandoned, where the abilities you have as a player are static throughout the whole game, compared to modern design that seems to take progression/customization of your abilities as a given?
label: analysis
